chunks: Humayd ibn Ziyad from al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Sama'ah from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan al-Mithamī from Aban ibn Uthman from Abu Baseer who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who killed a man deliberately, then the killer fled and they were not able to catch him. He (peace be upon him) said: 'If he had wealth, the blood money (diyah) would be taken from his wealth, and if not, then from the nearest [relative] to the nearest. If he had no relatives, the Imam would pay it, for the blood of a Muslim man would not be invalidated.'
And in another report: 'Then it is for the ruler afterwards to imprison him and discipline him.'

key_terms.الدِّيَةُ: Blood money or compensation paid to the victim or his heirs
key_terms.الْأَقْرَبِ فَالْأَقْرَبِ: The nearest to the nearest (referring to the hierarchy of kinship for financial liability)
key_terms.الْإِمَام: The Imam (in this context, the ruler or judge)

ai.seo_question: What is the hierarchy of paying blood money (diyah) for a deliberate murderer who flees in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi details the cascading liability for blood money (diyah) in cases of intentional homicide where the perpetrator is absent, reflecting the Shia juristic principle that the victim's right to compensation is never extinguished. It establishes a hierarchy of payment starting with the killer's personal assets, then his agnatic relatives, and ultimately the Imam (or the state treasury) as the final guarantor, ensuring social justice. The secondary narration highlights the ruler's discretionary authority to detain and discipline the fugitive, linking financial liability with judicial enforcement.
